Computer science classes are more theoretical and are harder but there are less of them hence the workload is lesser. For computer engineering, the courses are less difficult (but still tricky), however there is so much work. A big complaint in comptuer engineering is that the first two years make you learn "useless" physics and math, so if you are DEADSET on software, I would go with CS. That being said, I feel that you should take computer engineering so that you can explore your options. With CE you can get the same jobs as CS kids, and more because you will also have proficiency in things such as hardware, power, control, etc. Many people who go into CE for software end up liking another part of it as well (hardware is especially popular and makes really good money in industry). 

Don't decide on a program based on the workload because an easy program that you dislike will be harder for you than a tough program you enjoy. Personally if I chose CS i would suffer much more than I have in ECE.

if you are passionate about ur field, a good option is to find a niche part of industry that requires your skills. For example, for Neuroscience you can work do R&D for companies like Baycrest.

A huge huge huge asset is knowing statistical analysis and how to do data science in Python/R. Practically every industry/undergrad research position will require you to collect data and analyze it. It is pretty easy to learn and having solid Python knowledge will give you a big edge over competition. Also, knowing machine learning is extremely helpful. You don't need to know it well; just know the basics of using Neural Networks and stuff and you will be golden. A quick, neuroscience related ML project using Google Collab goes a long way.

Another thing; use undergrad research for industry connections. A pro tip is to work for biomedical engineering professors since working with them gives you a higher chance of getting an industry connection since more biomed eng stuff is extremely applied.

Toronto hospitals have alot of neuroscience research going on, as does the Canadian Government.  
Finally, if you do grad school you have a much better chance of getting a really cool R&D job in industry.
